statement: A straight line commensurable in length with a binomial straight line is itself also binomial and the same in order.
heath_proof: Let AB be binomial, and let CD be commensurable in length with AB; I say that CD is binomial and the same in order with AB. For, since AB is binomial, let it be divided into its terms at E, and let AE be the greater term; therefore AE, EB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. [X. 36] Let it be contrived that, as AB is to CD, so is AE to CF; [VI. 12] therefore also the remainder EB is to the remainder FD as AB is to CD. [V. 19] But AB is commensurable in length with CD; therefore AE is also commensurable with CF, and EB with FD. [X. 11] And AE, EB are rational; therefore CF, FD are also rational. And, as AE is to CF, so is EB to FD. [V. 11] Therefore, alternately, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD. [V. 16] But AE, EB are commensurable in square only; therefore CF, FD are also commensurable in square only. [X. 11] And they are rational; therefore CD is binomial. [X. 36] I say next that it is the same in order with AB. For the square on AE is greater than the square on EB either by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE or by the square on a straight line incommensurable with it. If then the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, the square on CF will also be greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line commensurable with CF. [X. 14] And, if AE is commensurable with the rational straight line set out, CF will also be commensurable with it, [X. 12] and for this reason each of the straight lines AB, CD is a first binomial, that is, the same in order. [X. Deff. II. 1] But, if EB is commensurable with the rational straight line set out, FD is also commensurable with it, [X. 12] and for this reason again CD will be the same in order with AB, for each of them will be a second binomial. [X. Deff. II. 2] But, if neither of the straight lines AE, EB is commensurable with the rational straight line set out, neither of the straight lines CF, FD will be commensurable with it, [X. 13] and each of the straight lines AB, CD is a third binomial. [X. Deff. II. 3] But, if the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, the square on CF is also greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CF. [X. 14] And, if AE is commensurable with the rational straight line set out, CF is also commensurable with it, and each of the straight lines AB, CD is a fourth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 4] But, if EB is so commensurable, so is FD also, and each of the straight lines AB, CD will be a fifth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 5] But, if neither of the straight lines AE, EB is so commensurable, neither of the straight lines CF, FD is commensurable with the rational straight line set out, and each of the straight lines AB, CD will be a sixth binomial. [X. Deff. II. 6] Hence a straight line commensurable in length with a binomial straight line is binomial and the same in order.

**Statement:** A straight line commensurable in length with a binomial straight line is itself also binomial and the same in order.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a binomial straight line, and let CD be commensurable in length with AB. We must show that CD is also binomial and of the same order as AB.

**Step 2.** Since AB is binomial, let it be divided into its terms at E, so that AE and EB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, with AE being the greater term [10.36]. Since the binomial is divided at one point only [10.42], this division is unique.

**Step 3.** Since CD is commensurable in length with AB, there is a ratio CD : AB which is the ratio of a number to a number [10.5]. Let CD : AB = p : q where p, q are numbers.

**Step 4.** Set CF : AE = p : q and FD : EB = p : q (i.e., CF : AE = CD : AB and FD : EB = CD : AB). Since AE + EB = AB and CF + FD = CF + FD, and CF/AE = FD/EB = CD/AB = p/q, we have CF + FD = (p/q)(AE + EB) = (p/q)(AB) = CD. So C, F, D are points on CD with CF + FD = CD [5.12, CN2].

**Step 5.** Since CF : AE = p : q, a ratio of number to number, CF is commensurable in length with AE [10.6]. Since AE is rational, CF is also rational [D10.1.3, 10.12].

**Step 6.** Since FD : EB = p : q, a ratio of number to number, FD is commensurable in length with EB [10.6]. Since EB is rational, FD is also rational [D10.1.3, 10.12].

**Step 7.** We now show CF and FD are commensurable in square only. Since CF is commensurable in length with AE, the square on CF is commensurable with the square on AE [10.11, 6.1]. Since FD is commensurable in length with EB, the square on FD is commensurable with the square on EB [10.11, 6.1].

**Step 8.** Suppose for contradiction that CF and FD are commensurable in length. Since CF is commensurable in length with AE, and FD is commensurable in length with EB, by transitivity AE would be commensurable in length with EB [10.12]. But AE and EB are commensurable in square only, contradicting commensurability in length. Therefore CF and FD are commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Since CF and FD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, CD = CF + FD is binomial [10.36].

**Step 10.** It remains to show CD is of the same order as AB. Since CF is commensurable in length with AE, the square on CF is commensurable with the square on AE [10.11]. Since FD is commensurable in length with EB, the square on FD is commensurable with the square on EB [10.11]. Therefore the square on CF minus the square on FD is commensurable with the square on AE minus the square on EB [CN3, 10.15].

**Step 11.** Since the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on some straight line G (say), and the square on CF is greater than the square on FD by the square on some straight line H, the square on G is to the square on H as it is commensurable with it, since both differences are commensurable [10.15].

**Step 12.** Consider the case where the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE. Since AE, CF are commensurable in length, and EB, FD are commensurable in length, and AE : EB :: CF : FD (since AE/CF = EB/FD = q/p), by 10.14 (the four lines AE, EB, CF, FD are proportional), the square on CF is also greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CF [10.14].

**Step 13.** Conversely, if the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, then by 10.14, the square on CF is greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with CF.

**Step 14.** Now let rho be a given rational straight line. For the order conditions: If AE is commensurable in length with rho, since CF is commensurable in length with AE, then CF is commensurable in length with rho [10.12]. If EB is commensurable in length with rho, since FD is commensurable in length with EB, then FD is commensurable in length with rho [10.12]. If neither AE nor EB is commensurable in length with rho, then since CF is commensurable in length with AE and FD is commensurable in length with EB, neither CF nor FD is commensurable in length with rho (for if CF were commensurable with rho, then AE would be too, by 10.12, contradiction; similarly for FD) [10.12].

**Step 15.** By the definitions of the six binomial orders [D10.2.1 through D10.2.6]: if AB is a first binomial (sq(AE) > sq(EB) by a square commensurable with AE, and AE commensurable with rho), then sq(CF) > sq(FD) by a square commensurable with CF, and CF is commensurable with rho, so CD is a first binomial. The same reasoning applies to each of the remaining five orders, since both the commensurability condition on the difference of squares and the commensurability of the terms with the rational line are preserved.

**Step 16.** Therefore CD is binomial and of the same order as AB. Q.E.D.
